title: Hyperbrowser Alternatives: 8 Options Compared
summary: Eight Hyperbrowser alternatives grouped by the layer you're replacing: cloud browsers, self-hosted browsers, agent frameworks and workflow platforms.
body_markdown:
You might be looking for a Hyperbrowser alternative because running thousands of jobs is costing more than you planned. Maybe you need browsers inside your own network to reach private apps. Or maybe you need a tool to manage a complete business workflow.


We build Skyvern, an AI browser automation platform that lets operations teams handle recurring portal tasks, such as downloading invoices from vendor websites, without writing code. So we know what it takes to run these workflows in production.


In this article, we compare eight alternatives, covering managed browser services, self-hosted browsers, agent frameworks, and workflow platforms, including Skyvern. We look at what each tool does and how it charges. We also give you a checklist to help you see how the differences affect your workflow before switching.


## Hyperbrowser in brief: what it does and what it costs


Hyperbrowser sells cloud Chrome sessions for AI agents, plus sandboxes, a fetch-and-crawl API, and hosted agents. It has a free plan with 5,000 credits, and paid plans start at $30 a month.


Hyperbrowser runs and scales the browsers, which you can control with your own Playwright or Puppeteer code. Selenium support is available by email request. You can also send prompts to hosted agents, including HyperAgent (Hyperbrowser’s own open-source agent framework), Browser Use, and computer-use models. Its MCP server lets AI assistants that support the Model Context Protocol control the browsers.


Hyperbrowser also handles logins and replays. Its browsers keep profiles with saved cookies and logins, and you can watch sessions live or replay them. Since October 2026, it has been able to store a password, a TOTP seed for two-factor codes, or a 1Password secret, and type it into a login form without the value reaching your code or the model. HyperAgent can also record the actions of an AI run and replay them later without calling the model.


Plan Price Included usage Concurrent sessions


Free $0 5,000 credits ($5) 1


Startup $30/month 30,000 credits ($30) 25


Scale $100/month 100,000 credits ($100) 100


Enterprise Custom Custom 1,000+


Hyperbrowser’s products share a credit balance, and the standard price is $1 per 1,000 credits. Browser time costs $0.10 an hour, and proxy data costs $10 per GB. The hosted agents, HyperAgent and Browser Use, add $0.02 per step on top of the browser time, and fetching a page costs $0.001. The paid plans include automatic CAPTCHA solving, basic stealth mode, and residential proxies. Plan credits reset every month, and unused ones don't carry over.


Proxy data can be the biggest line on the bill. Ten hours of browser time cost $1, while 1 GB of proxy traffic costs $10.


## What these tools cover


Browser automation tools cover different parts of the job. Browser hosting provides the browsers, either in a vendor’s cloud or on your own infrastructure, while an agent framework controls their actions. A workflow platform combines browser actions with login handling, scheduling, and file downloads to carry out a business process.


## The 8 Hyperbrowser alternatives


### 1. Skyvern


Skyvern runs business workflows on websites your team logs into. One workflow can sign in, enter the two-factor code, fill a multi-page form, and download the result, then do it again every night on a[schedule](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/sdk-reference/schedules) . Examples include[downloading invoices from vendor portals](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/how-to-automate-downloading-invoices-september-2025/) ,[checking patient eligibility](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automating-healthcare-insurance-eligibility-verification/) on payer portals such as Availity and UHC Provider, and submitting job applications across applicant tracking systems. Skyvern automates browsers only, so desktop applications are out of its scope.


The people who do this work can build the workflow themselves. Skyvern's Copilot drafts it from a plain-English description, an uploaded SOP, or a recording of someone doing the task ([Studio docs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/studio) ). An engineer connects it to the rest of the stack through the API or the[MCP server](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/developers/getting-started/mcp) , which works on every plan.


- **Logins and 2FA:** stored credentials work on every plan, and the credential vault is never exposed to the model ([products](https://www.skyvern.com/products) ). Email codes and magic links have no plan gate. Authenticator-app (TOTP) codes need Pro, a Skyvern phone number for SMS codes costs $10 a month on Pro, and passkeys require an Enterprise plan and a connected Bitwarden account ([credentials docs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/credentials) ,[pricing](https://www.skyvern.com/pricing) ).
- **When a page changes:** after the first run, Skyvern caches the steps as Playwright code, so repeat runs skip the model. If the cached code fails because the page changed, AI fallback, which is on by default, hands the step back to the agent and regenerates the code ([browser automation docs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/developers/browser-automation) ).
- **A record of every run:** each run keeps a recording, a screenshot of each step, and a timeline ([runs docs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/runs) ).
- **Browser sessions on their own:** Skyvern also sells cloud browser sessions without the agent. Your Playwright code connects over the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), and the session is billed as browser uptime, at 200 credits an hour ([browser sessions docs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/sdk-reference/browser-sessions) ).


**Pricing:** Skyvern's Hobby plan costs $29 a month for 30,000 credits and 10 concurrent agents. Pro is $149 a month for 150,000 credits and 25 concurrent agents. Both come with a 14-day free trial, and Enterprise is custom ([pricing](https://www.skyvern.com/pricing) ).


Credits pay for what the browser does, and 1 credit is $0.001. Skyvern charges 30 credits per AI action, 15 credits per cached action, 10 credits to read a one-time login code from an email or text message, and 200 credits per hour of browser uptime ([account and billing docs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/account) ). For example, a run with 12 AI actions, 1 emailed code, and 3 minutes of browser time comes to 380 credits, or $0.38. Once its steps are cached, the same run costs 200 credits.


Our[Hyperbrowser vs Skyvern comparison](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/hyperbrowser-ai-vs-skyvern/) goes deeper, and[Skyvern MCP vs Hyperbrowser](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/skyvern-mcp-vs-hyperbrowser-ai/) compares the two MCP servers.


### 2. Browserbase


Browserbase sells a similar set of products to Hyperbrowser's: cloud browsers, hosted agents you start from a prompt, search and fetch APIs, a sandboxed runtime for agent code, and a login product called Identity. It also maintains[Stagehand](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/stagehand-alternatives-pricing-reviews/) , an MIT-licensed framework that adds AI commands to browser automation code.


**Pricing:** the free plan includes 1 browser hour, 3 concurrent browsers, and sessions of up to 15 minutes. Developer costs $20 a month and includes 100 browser hours and 1 GB of proxy data. Additional usage costs $0.12 per browser hour and $12 per GB of proxy data. Startup costs $99 a month for 500 browser hours, with additional hours at $0.10 each. CAPTCHA solving and basic stealth start on Developer.


See our[Browserbase vs Hyperbrowser comparison](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/browserbase-vs-hyperbrowser-ai/) .


### 3. Steel


Steel runs managed cloud browsers and publishes its browser, Steel Browser, as open source under the Apache-2.0 license. You can start on Steel's cloud and run the same browser on your own machines later.


**Pricing:** the Launch plan has no monthly fee. It comes with $30 of one-time credits, then charges $0.10 a browser hour, with 10 concurrent sessions of up to 15 minutes each. Scale is $250 a month with $100 of credits a month and $0.08 a browser hour, and its sessions can last up to 1 hour.


See our[Steel review](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/steel-reviews-pricing-alternatives/) .


### 4. Kernel


Kernel runs cloud browsers and bills them for memory used per second, with no charge for idle time or proxy traffic. Its free plan includes live view, stealth mode with a Kernel-managed proxy and a CAPTCHA solver, and managed auth, which signs agents in to sites and keeps them signed in.


**Pricing:** usage costs $0.0000166667 per GB-second, which comes to about $0.06 an hour for a default headless browser. The free plan adds $5 of credits a month, 5 concurrent browsers, 3 managed-auth connections, and 1 day of session replays. Hobbyist is $30 a month with $10 of credits, 10 concurrent browsers, and 7 days of replays. Live view and replays require headful browsers, which cost about $0.48 an hour at Kernel’s per-second rate.


Our[Browserbase vs Kernel comparison](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/browserbase-vs-kernel-which-is-better/) covers Kernel in depth.


### 5. Browserless


Browserless hosts headless Chrome, Firefox, and WebKit browsers that your Playwright or Puppeteer scripts connect to. It also offers REST APIs for screenshots and PDFs, and its own query language, BrowserQL.


**Pricing:** Browserless bills in units, and 1 unit is up to 30 seconds of browser time per connection. The free plan includes 1,000 units a month, 2 concurrent browsers, and sessions of up to 2 minutes. Prototyping is $25 a month, billed yearly, for 20,000 units, which is about 166 browser hours, with sessions of up to 15 minutes.


**Self-hosting:** the Browserless Docker image is free for non-commercial use under the SSPL license. Commercial or closed-source use needs a commercial license, which the Enterprise plan includes.


### 6. Anchor Browser


Anchor Browser runs cloud browsers built around logged-in agent work, with an authentication product for computer-use agents called OmniConnect. Anchor uses AI to plan a browser task once, then runs the task as deterministic code, and falls back to AI only when a run needs it.


**Pricing:** the free plan includes 5 credits a month and up to 5 concurrent browsers. Starter is $50 a month for 50 credits and up to 25 concurrent browsers, with logged-in browsers and CAPTCHA handling. Enterprise adds bring-your-own-cloud and on-premises deployment.


See our[Anchor Browser alternatives guide](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/anchorbrowser-alternatives-pricing-reviews/) .


### 7. Browser Use


Browser Use is an open-source Python library for browser agents, under the MIT license, with its own cloud for browsers and models. You can run Browser Use on your own machines or use a hosted service such as Hyperbrowser. The three options differ in who manages the browsers and how usage is billed:


- **Run the library yourself.** It's free on your own machines with the model provider you choose, and you manage the browsers.
- **Use Browser Use Cloud.** It charges $0.02 per browser hour and $5 per GB of home-IP proxy traffic, with CAPTCHA solving included and no subscription. It also sells its own models, BU Fast and BU Ultrafast, which the library reaches through` ChatBrowserUse` .
- **Run it on Hyperbrowser.** You pay $0.02 per step, plus Hyperbrowser's browser time and proxy data, and the browsers and recordings sit in the same account as your other Hyperbrowser work.


Our[Browser Use alternatives guide](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/browser-use-alternatives/) compares it with other agent frameworks.


### 8. Airtop


Airtop starts by researching your business and developing a plan for automating sales and marketing work. It then builds AI agents to carry out tasks such as outreach, lead research, and ad monitoring.


**Pricing:** the free plan includes 1,000 credits and 3 simultaneous sessions, and Starter is $29 a month for 30,000 credits.


See our[Airtop review](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/airtop-reviews-pricing-alternatives/) .

## How to test an alternative before you switch


Run your hardest real target on two candidates for a day before you migrate, because session start time, stealth, logins, and debugging behave differently on every site. Check these on both:


- **Your existing code.** Point your Playwright, Puppeteer, or Selenium scripts at the new vendor. If you use Selenium, confirm support first, since Hyperbrowser enables it by email request.
- **Session start and persistence.** Time a session start from your own region with your proxy settings. Check whether a saved profile keeps you signed in across runs and how long a session can last on the plan you'd buy.
- **CAPTCHAs and bot checks.** Test both tools on sites you're authorized to automate, on the plan you'd pay for, because CAPTCHA solving and stealth differ by plan for most of these vendors.
- **Logins with 2FA.** List the second factors your target sites use, such as authenticator codes, email, SMS, magic links, or passkeys, and check which ones the vendor handles and on which plan.
- **Failed runs.** Break a run on purpose and see whether the recording, logs, and live view tell you enough to fix it.
- **Cost on one real run.** Credit systems differ, so compare dollars on the same job. Hyperbrowser charges per browser-hour plus $0.02 per agent step, Skyvern per action and per browser-hour, Kernel per GB-second of memory, and Browserless per 30-second unit.


## Try Skyvern on your own portal workflow


Use your test runs to assess what a move from Hyperbrowser would mean for your team. Managed browser services, self-hosted browsers, agent frameworks, and workflow platforms handle different parts of the job, so compare what you would need to build and maintain alongside the cost of each completed task.


Skyvern lets your operations team build recurring portal workflows from a plain-English description, an SOP, or a recording. Try automating a task like downloading invoices from a vendor portal, then compare the results with your current process.


Start[Skyvern's 14-day free trial](https://www.skyvern.com/pricing) to test it as a Hyperbrowser alternative on that workflow. Check whether it completes the task from login to downloaded file, then review the run recording and credit usage before moving more work across.


## FAQ


### Is Hyperbrowser free?


Yes. Hyperbrowser's free plan includes 5,000 credits, worth $5 of usage, with 1 concurrent session and 7 days of data retention. Hyperbrowser says that's enough for about 50 browser hours at base rates. When the credits run out, you upgrade to a paid plan to keep going.


### Which Hyperbrowser alternatives are open source?


Skyvern’s open-source version (AGPL-3.0) covers the workflow layer. Steel Browser is open source under Apache-2.0 and runs on your own machines, while Browser Use provides an MIT-licensed agent library. Browserless’s Docker image is free for non-commercial use but needs a commercial license otherwise.


### Does Hyperbrowser have an MCP server?


Yes. Hyperbrowser publishes an MCP server next to its Node.js and Python SDKs, so an AI assistant that supports MCP can use its browsers. Skyvern has one too, and[Skyvern MCP vs Hyperbrowser](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/skyvern-mcp-vs-hyperbrowser-ai/) compares them.


### Is there a Hyperbrowser alternative for non-developers?


Yes. Skyvern lets operations teams build workflows without writing code. They can describe the task to Copilot, upload an SOP, or record the task once. Airtop offers agents for sales and marketing teams.
